irac_C1.issue: The issue is whether benefit-sharing obligations under the Nagoya Protocol extend to the downstream commercialization of marine genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, even when the initial access was granted for non-commercial research.

rules_selected.text: In accordance with Article 15, paragraphs 3 and 7 of the Convention, benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources as well as subsequent applications and commercialization shall be shared in a fair and equitable way with the Party providing such resources that is the country of origin of such resources or a Party that has acquired the genetic resources in accordance with the Convention. Such sharing shall be upon mutually agreed terms.

Each Party shall take legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, in order that the benefits arising from the utilization of traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources are shared in a fair and equitable way with indigenous and local communities holding such knowledge. Such sharing shall be upon mutually agreed terms.

In the development and implementation of its access and benefit-sharing legislation or regulatory requirements, each Party shall: (a) Create conditions to promote and encourage research which contributes to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity, particularly in developing countries, including through simplified measures on access for non-commercial research purposes, taking into account the need to address a change of intent for such research;

Pursuant to paragraph 1 above, each Party requiring prior informed consent shall take the necessary legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, to: ... (g) Establish clear rules and procedures for requiring and establishing mutually agreed terms. Such terms shall be set out in writing and may include, inter alia: (i) A dispute settlement clause; (ii) Terms on benefit-sharing, including in relation to intellectual property rights; (iii) Terms on subsequent third-party use, if any; and (iv) Terms on changes of intent, where applicable.

Each Party shall take appropriate, effective and proportionate legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, to provide that traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources utilized within their jurisdiction has been accessed in accordance with prior informed consent or approval and involvement of indigenous and local communities and that mutually agreed terms have been established, as required by domestic access and benefit-sharing legislation or regulatory requirements of the other Party where such indigenous and local communities are located.

irac_C1.analysis:
The conclusion that benefit-sharing obligations extend to downstream commercial uses is strongly supported by the foundational principles and specific obligations within the Nagoya Protocol. The core of the obligation is found in NAGOYA_M003, which mandates that benefits from the “utilization of genetic resources as well as subsequent applications and commercialization shall be shared.” This language explicitly contemplates a value chain that extends beyond initial access. The facts confirm that the Peruvian pharmaceutical company’s development of commercial products constitutes “subsequent applications and commercialization” of the MGRs initially accessed by the research institution. Similarly, NAGOYA_M006 requires that benefits from the “utilization of traditional knowledge” be shared with the Indigenous community. The company’s work, which is based on the initial research guided by this TK, is a form of utilization, triggering this obligation.

The initial “non-commercial” designation of the project does not extinguish these downstream duties. NAGOYA_M019 permits “simplified measures on access for non-commercial research purposes,” but critically qualifies this by requiring Parties to take “into account the need to address a change of intent for such research.” The transition from publicly funded research to the development of patented commercial products by a pharmaceutical company is a clear “change of intent.” This provision signals that a non-commercial access agreement cannot serve as a loophole to avoid benefit-sharing upon commercialization. This links directly to the duties of the provider state, Brazil. Under NAGOYA_M015, Brazil has a duty to “Establish clear rules and procedures for requiring and establishing mutually agreed terms,” which may include terms on “subsequent third-party use” and “changes of intent.” The fact that the MAT were limited and did not include such terms suggests a failure in Brazil’s implementation of this duty, rather than a negation of the underlying principle. Finally, Peru, as the user country, has its own compliance duties. NAGOYA_M048 obligates Peru to ensure that TK “utilized within their jurisdiction” has been accessed correctly and that MAT were established as required by Brazil’s domestic law. The commercialization by the Peruvian company triggers this checkpoint duty, requiring Peru to ensure the entire utilization pathway, including the new commercial intent, complies with the principles of fair and equitable benefit-sharing.

irac_C2.issue: The issue is whether benefit-sharing obligations are limited by the initial non-commercial access agreement, thereby not extending to downstream commercialization by a third party where the mutually agreed terms did not provide for it.

rules_selected.text: In accordance with Article 15, paragraphs 3 and 7 of the Convention, benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources as well as subsequent applications and commercialization shall be shared in a fair and equitable way with the Party providing such resources that is the country of origin of such resources or a Party that has acquired the genetic resources in accordance with the Convention. Such sharing shall be upon mutually agreed terms.

Each Party shall take legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, in order that the benefits arising from the utilization of traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources are shared in a fair and equitable way with indigenous and local communities holding such knowledge. Such sharing shall be upon mutually agreed terms.

Pursuant to paragraph 1 above, each Party requiring prior informed consent shall take the necessary legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, to: ... (e) Provide for the issuance at the time of access of a permit or its equivalent as evidence of the decision to grant prior informed consent and of the establishment of mutually agreed terms, and notify the Access and Benefit-sharing Clearing-House accordingly;

Each Party shall take appropriate, effective and proportionate legislative, administrative or policy measures to provide that genetic resources utilized within its jurisdiction have been accessed in accordance with prior informed consent and that mutually agreed terms have been established, as required by the domestic access and benefit-sharing legislation or regulatory requirements of the other Party.

Each Party shall take appropriate, effective and proportionate legislative, administrative or policy measures, as appropriate, to provide that traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources utilized within their jurisdiction has been accessed in accordance with prior informed consent or approval and involvement of indigenous and local communities and that mutually agreed terms have been established, as required by domestic access and benefit-sharing legislation or regulatory requirements of the other Party where such indigenous and local communities are located.

irac_C2.analysis:
The conclusion that benefit-sharing obligations do not automatically extend to downstream commercial uses is grounded in the central role of mutually agreed terms (MAT) and the deference to domestic legislation. Both NAGOYA_M003, concerning genetic resources, and NAGOYA_M006, concerning associated traditional knowledge, establish that benefit-sharing “shall be upon mutually agreed terms.” This phrase is not merely procedural; it defines the scope and content of the obligation. The duty to share benefits is not an abstract, free-floating requirement but one that is crystallized and given legal effect through the specific terms negotiated and agreed upon by the parties. In this case, the facts explicitly state that “mutually agreed terms are limited to standard reporting obligations, and no benefit-sharing mechanisms are triggered at the point of access.” Because the parties did not agree to terms covering commercialization or third-party use, no such obligation was created under the agreement.

The finality of the initial access arrangement is reinforced by NAGOYA_M013, which requires the provider Party to issue a permit “at the time of access as evidence of the decision to grant prior informed consent and of the establishment of mutually agreed terms.” This frames the access and benefit-sharing arrangement as a discrete event, concluded and evidenced by the permit. The facts confirm that access was “authorised by Brazil’s national competent authority,” implying that Brazil fulfilled this duty and considered the established MAT to be sufficient at that time.

Furthermore, the obligations of the user country, Peru, are explicitly conditioned on the laws of the provider country, Brazil. NAGOYA_M045 requires Peru to ensure that MGRs were accessed and MAT established “as required by the domestic access and benefit-sharing legislation or regulatory requirements of the other Party.” Likewise, NAGOYA_M048 imposes a similar duty for TK. Since Brazil’s competent authority authorized the access as non-commercial without requiring downstream tracking, Peru can reasonably conclude that the initial access was compliant with Brazilian law. The facts state the project “was never required to track downstream uses or disclose transitions,” indicating that the legal framework under which access was granted did not impose such a prospective duty. Therefore, from Peru’s perspective, there is no non-compliance to address, as the utilization by the pharmaceutical company is based on research that was, at its inception, fully compliant with the provider country’s requirements as expressed in the authorized MAT.
